On Oct 20 the company pre-announced revenue of $18.5B–$19.5B, against earlier guidance of $14.5B–$15.5B. It also pre-announced gross margin of 12.0%–12.5%, against a prior 10.4%–10.8% range (Read more, Nov 3, 2026).

Super Micro Computer (SMCI): Trading at $31.70 (+4.12%, as of Nov 3, 3:48 PM EST) || Market cap: $20.74B || 1M: -27.29% || 52-week range: $19.48–$51.40

Stale consensus alert

The earnings-calendar consensus still shows EPS $1.04 and revenue $14.78B. That sits at the old guidance, not the pre-announcement. The FinQL forward estimate (as of Nov 3, 2026) is slightly higher at $15.02B revenue and $1.24 EPS. Headline "beats" against these figures will therefore be largely baked in. The real question is how the results compare with the pre-announced range and with the next-quarter outlook.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

What to watch

Margin durability. Gross margin of 12.0%–12.5% was credited to "favorable customer and product mix." If management calls that one-off, the bull case weakens. Note that FinQL's last-quarter gross margin reading (17.5%, as of Jun 30, 2026) doesn't fit the narrative figures. Treat it with caution until the filing arrives.

Guidance versus the Street. Consensus has Dec-quarter revenue at $18.11B and FY2027 at $73.03B. In August, management guided FY2027 to $65B–$72B. A raise above $73B would validate the pre-announcement. A hold would suggest Q1 pulled demand forward.

Working capital and funding. On the May call, management said doubling revenue again might require outside capital. Watch inventory, cash conversion and any financing talk.

Legal overhang. A March 19 DOJ indictment over alleged illegal AI-server exports to China cut shares 33% the next day. Co-founder Wally Liam resigned from the board. Any investigation update could outweigh the numbers.

Super Micro: Fiscal Q1 Earnings Snapshot
Associated Press
Tue, November 3, 2026 at 4:19 PM EST 1 min read
SMCI
Trade SMCI on Coinbase

SAN JOSE, Calif. (AP) — SAN JOSE, Calif. (AP) — Super Micro Computer Inc. (SMCI) on Tuesday reported fiscal first-quarter profit of $1.59 billion.

On a per-share basis, the San Jose, California-based company said it had net income of $1.75. Earnings, adjusted for one-time gains and costs, were $1.81 per share.

The results topped Wall Street expectations. The average estimate of seven analysts surveyed by Zacks Investment Research was for earnings of $1.24 per share.

The server technology company posted revenue of $19.95 billion in the period, also beating Street forecasts. Five analysts surveyed by Zacks expected $15.77 billion.

For the current quarter ending in December, Super Micro expects its per-share earnings to range from $1.66 to $1.90.

The company said it expects revenue in the range of $19.5 billion to $21.5 billion for the fiscal second quarter.

Super Micro expects full-year revenue in the range of $72 billion to $82 billion.

Key Takeaways

Celestica stock is down 36% in the past month, even though it beat its own third-quarter guidance and forecast $40.0 billion of revenue for 2027.

Celestica fell with the rest of the AI hardware group, including Dell and Super Micro, and had no bad news of its own.

The main risk is cash: Celestica cut its 2026 free cash flow outlook to $460 million and plans $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion of capital spending in 2027.

Analysts' estimates and targets have held up through the drop, and if the 2027 outlook holds, the sell-off looks like an overreaction.

Celestica (CLS) stock is down 36% in the past month, and Celestica gave investors very little reason to sell. Its third-quarter results beat the top of its own guidance, and its first outlook for 2027 calls for 90% revenue growth.

It got caught in a sell-off of AI hardware stocks instead. It fell alongside Flex and Sanmina on Oct. 22 with no news of its own. Over the month, Dell Technologies lost 30% and Super Micro Computer 29%, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 9%.

Wall Street hasn't wavered. On Oct. 29, CIBC analyst Todd Coupland kept his Buy rating and $500 price target, 101% above Monday's close.

Celestica reported after the close on Oct. 26, and the numbers beat both its own guidance and Wall Street's:

Adjusted EPS of $3.30, up 109%, against $2.96

A record adjusted operating margin of 8.5%

Chair and CEO Rob Mionis went further in the release: "The demand environment continues to be very robust, supporting our 2027 revenue outlook, with customer demand forecasts meaningfully higher for 2028."

The stock jumped 12% the next day and gave it back within a week. Analysts now expect normalized EPS to nearly double again in 2027, to $22.24, a touch above the company's own $21.50 guide:

CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) jumped 5% today, and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) rose 4%, after Oracle priced $20 billion of new stock and bonds late Monday.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) rose 4% and Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) 4%, and Cipher Digital (CIFR:NASDAQ) jumped 16%.

Exactly what Oracle said it would do

Oracle is selling 86.2 million shares at $116 apiece, plus $10 billion of notes with coupons of 7% to 8.65%. That fits the roughly $40 billion it said in June it would raise in fiscal 2027.

Baird analyst Rob Oliver said the sale "seems to be exactly what they previewed."

CoreWeave pays a lot more for its money

Analysts expect CoreWeave's revenue to climb from $5.13 billion in 2025 to $26.5 billion in 2027:

CoreWeave (CRWV): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2025-2028 (TIKR)

Oracle's raise shouldn't move those estimates, but CoreWeave must borrow to hit them: consensus sees negative free cash flow every year through 2030.

And it pays more than Oracle does. Its last two unsecured bond deals came at 9.75% in April and 9.625% in June, and its 9.625% notes due 2032 traded at a yield near 15% in mid-October.

The stock trades like investors doubt it will get that money. CoreWeave closed Monday at 1.4x forward sales, its low for the past year and well under its 3.6x average:

AMD supplies the MI450 chips for Oracle's planned 50,000-GPU cluster. Super Micro agreed this morning to build SambaNova inference racks, starting with 10,000 chips. Their reports tonight will show whether money like Oracle's is still turning into orders.

After Cipher's third-quarter report Monday, JPMorgan cut its target to $18 from $22. Cipher needs tenants to keep signing leases, and Keefe, Bruyette & Woods warned that new ones could dry up.

title: 3 Stocks That Did Well the Last Time the Fed Raised Rates Aggressively
detail:
3 Stocks That Did Well the Last Time the Fed Raised Rates Aggressively
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 3, 2026 at 2:51 PM EST 5 min read
XOM
MRK
SMCI
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The Federal Reserve recently raised interest rates for the first time in years, and more rate hikes are expected. Another hike may even happen before the end of the year. How much higher rates end up going is anyone's guess at this point, as inflation remains elevated and the war in Iran doesn't appear to be ending anytime soon.

For investors, now may be a good time to consider investments that may do well even amid adversity. Three stocks that did well the last time the Fed aggressively raised interest rates in 2022 include ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), Merck (NYSE:MRK), and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI). Here's how they did back then, and whether these stocks can once again prove to be good buys right now.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

ExxonMobil

Oil and gas giant ExxonMobil generated exceptional returns of more than 80% back in 2022, which was impressive given that the S&P 500 declined by more than 19%, in what proved to be a disastrous year for the markets. The company is a leader in the oil and gas sector and benefits from rising oil prices, which were soaring in 2022. Now, they're also at elevated levels, and once again, ExxonMobil's stock is a hot buy – it's up around 50% this year.

Investing in the company can be a good way for investors to hedge against overall market risk, because if inflation is high and interest rates are rising, ExxonMobil's business may do better than most due to rising commodity prices.

Another great reason to consider buying the stock is its dividend, which currently yields 2.4% – that's double the S&P 500 average of 1.1%. Plus, ExxonMobil has been increasing its payout for decades. With strong earnings and a leadership position in the industry, the company's financials are likely to improve, and it will be able to continue raising its dividend for the foreseeable future.

Merck

Another stock that did well in 2022 was healthcare company Merck, whose shares rose by 45%. The healthcare industry can be a fairly insulated area of the economy, as pharmaceutical drugs and medical devices are consistently in high demand and generally don't depend on the economic cycle. That can make investing in these types of companies fairly safe moves for investors.

Merck had a strong year in 2022, with sales rising 22% and its leading cancer drug, Keytruda, growing at the same rate. The company's operations are robust, and with its drugs in high demand, Merck performed well even as other stocks struggled. While it's not a guarantee that every healthcare stock will perform better in a downturn, it's a great example of the safety the sector can offer.

Super Micro Fell 7% on a Memory Shortage Warning. Its Margin Has to Answer November 3 ©@Tiero via Canva
Key Takeaways

Super Micro fell 7% on Friday along with Dell and other hardware stocks, after Intel warned that memory prices and shortages are slowing PC demand.

Super Micro sells no PCs. It has already said its September-quarter gross margin should come in at 12.0%-12.5%, above its own 10.4%-10.8% forecast.

Intel's warning covers recent weeks, so the memory test on Nov. 3 is Super Micro's December-quarter margin outlook. Analysts expect a 10.2% gross margin for fiscal 2027.

At 6.9x forward earnings, near its five-year low, the stock already prices in a squeeze. A margin outlook near 10% and an unchanged fiscal 2027 sales range would make the drop look overdone.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) fell 7% on Friday after Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) warned that memory shortages are choking PC demand. The selling ran through the hardware makers: Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE) fell 11%, and HP and Hewlett Packard Enterprise dropped too.

Super Micro reports its fiscal first-quarter results after the close on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Gross margin is where a memory squeeze would show up first.

Intel blamed memory for a PC slowdown

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan laid out the problem on Intel's earnings call on Oct. 29: "In recent weeks, our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability." Intel's stock fell 29% the next day.

That's a PC problem first. Dell's PC business takes the direct hit. But its AI server business came into Friday with a $95 billion backlog, after record AI orders of $60.9 billion and a raised fiscal 2027 revenue outlook of $192 billion.

Super Micro sells no PCs. Daniel Niles of Satori Fund wrote on X on Sunday that "I am not a fan of SuperMicro to be clear." In the same post, he described its revenue as "purely enterprise related."

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Super Micro Computer, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Super Micro Computer's Analyst Ratings

The September quarter is mostly in the books

On Oct. 20, Super Micro said it expects September-quarter revenue of $18.5 billion-$19.5 billion, against guidance of $14.5 billion-$15.5 billion. It put gross margin at 12.0%-12.5%, up from the 10.4%-10.8% it had forecast.

So the quarter it reports on Nov. 3 is largely known. It also ended Sept. 30, before the "recent weeks" Tan described. That makes the December-quarter outlook the real memory test.
